prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, bringing optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from circuit QED (B023) to the optical lattice clock (B043) as a single part. The magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea: it removes Doppler, recoil and first-order light-shift errors while interrogating many atoms at once, which the 2005 comb and 2012 single-ion prizes did not do. The step from there to the 1e-18 regime and to the many-body clock physics of dense spin-polarised fermions is a physics result, not only a refinement, and it has been confirmed independently in Sr, Yb and Hg and by direct clock comparisons. The attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori for the concept and first strontium lattice clock, Ye for the record accuracy and the many-body understanding. It is also the only candidate that most of the committee already ranks or lists as an alternative, and I weigh that only as a sign that no one disputes the evidence. What decided it for me is that, in round 1, every real obstacle to B023 was one that cannot be solved inside three names, and that the clock does not carry that problem. I also have a proximity issue on B023 that I would rather not carry into a prize decision.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to B043 is the one I raised myself in round 1: it is precision metrology, and some will read it as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes rather than a discovery of new physics. The pending redefinition of the second has not happened, and no deviation from existing theory has been seen. Two names also leave out Lemonde, Pfau, the Paris and Braunschweig groups and the wider Boulder team. A single-part prize is also a narrower statement than a two-part prize, and I give up the argument that circuit QED opened a new regime of light-matter physics, which I still believe.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the lattice clock is a measurement breakthrough with a clear before and after, a clean Katori and Ye attribution, and a prize that rewards demonstrated 1e-18 performance, not the future redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I accept this framing and I now stand with it. Where I pressed you in round 1 was that the clock is refinement and not discovery. On reflection the lattice concept changes the statistical regime of the measurement, and the many-body clock physics from the Ye group is a physics yield that goes beyond the frequency-standard programme. I agree the citation should name the demonstrated performance and not the redefinition of the second. I also note your disclosure of a research stay in Hall's laboratory; I see no documented tie to Katori or Ye, and I defer to the chair on whether it matters.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the clock is a single well-defined achievement, confirmed independently, not recognised by earlier prizes on the comb and ion clocks, with Lemonde, Pfau and the Boulder group as the allocation problem.
responses.response: This is the argument that moved me most. The distinction from 2005 and 2012 is real: the comb provided the ruler and the ion clocks provided the single-quantum-system control, while the lattice solved the problem of combining many atoms with a cancelled light shift. I agree the allocation to two names is the main residual weakness, but the two names map onto the concept (Katori) and the record accuracy (Ye), and I do not see a better three-name cut that adds Lemonde or Pfau without diluting the case.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, supports a two-part prize pairing B043 with IceCube credited to Halzen alone, and sees the IceCube discovery as secure while attribution is the stated obstacle.
responses.response: My round-1 question to you on the decisive individual contribution has not been answered by anyone, and you concede that the lone name is the weak point. A one-name half beside a two-name half invites the objection that the committee picked a figurehead from a collaboration of hundreds, and Karle and Yoshida have comparable claims on detector and analysis leadership. For that reason I would prefer the clock alone to the pairing. I would reconsider only if members who know the IceCube history can show a contribution to the 2013 diffuse-flux result that is separable from Karle's and Yoshida's.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks gamma-ray bursts and IceCube highest on discovery grounds, but says he would drop the IceCube half rather than invent an artificial trio if no clean credit exists.
responses.response: That is the right test, and by it I think the IceCube half fails this year, because a lone name or a three-name cut will look arbitrary to a large part of the community. Your own statement that the clock is the best supported part, with a clean two-person attribution and a measurable consequence, is close to my reason for moving to B043 alone. If the committee does want a second part, I do not think B010 is the answer without a resolved credit, and I would rather examine B029 or B008 for that role in a later year than force a pairing now.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as a theory-then-experiment discovery, and lists the clock only as an alternative because of what new physics it teaches.
responses.response: I take the theory-plus-experiment structure seriously, and my objection to B029 remains maturity: the pairing mechanism is unsettled, the experiments date from 2018, and Cao, Fatemi, Dean and the earlier Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto theory complicate the three-name cut. A citation that names only the flat bands and correlated states would answer part of it, but I think the field will be better served by waiting for a settled mechanism. As to your own question about what new physics the clock teaches, my answer is that it gives a tested many-body understanding of dense fermion clocks and a platform for tests of constants and relativistic geodesy.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers topological insulators for combining discovery-level originality with the broadest independent confirmation and tight theory-experiment linkage, and sees the clock as a possible refinement.
responses.response: The Kane-Mele and Molenkamp pairing is the cleanest theory-and-experiment case among the condensed-matter candidates, and I agree the confirmation is broad. My difficulty is the overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases, which you raise yourself, and the unresolved Hasan or Mele or Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang question, which no three-name cut resolves. The clock has no equivalent attribution problem inside the two names, and I think the timing is stronger.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a discovery or as refinement of precision metrology, and whether the redefinition of the second should delay it.
Whether two names for B043 leave out Lemonde, Pfau, and other groups too visibly.
Whether a single-part prize is better than a two-part prize if a clean credit for a second achievement, such as IceCube, can be identified.
statement.conflict_note: I direct WACQT and work at Chalmers on superconducting circuits and circuit and waveguide QED, and my Chalmers colleagues and the 2025 laureates' visit connect me to that community. I have moved away from B023 and, if it is considered, I should be treated as potentially conflicted on it, including as an alternative. I have no documented collaboration or relationship with Katori, Ye or the other B043 groups in my profile, and I note Olsson's mention of me as a Chalmers colleague, though no shortlisted ballot credits a Chalmers person.
